title: Understanding the basics of agility: Scrum, Kanban, XP
content:
Introduction: Why agility has revolutionized development

Agility was born from an overwhelming observation: 70% of IT projects failed in the 90s-2000s because of methods that were too rigid (V-shaped cycle, waterfall). The Agile Manifesto (2001), created by 17 visionary developers, established 4 fundamental values:
  • Individuals and their interactions > processes and tools
  • Functional software > exhaustive documentation
  • Collaboration with the client > contractual negotiation
  • Adapting to change > following a rigid plan
These principles have given rise to several complementary frameworks.

1️⃣ Scrum: the most used framework in the world

Fundamentals

Scrum is based on short cycles called sprints (usually 2 weeks, sometimes 1 or 3). Each sprint aims to deliver a potentially shippable product increment.

The 3 key roles (and their actual responsibilities)

Product Owner (PO)
  • Drives the product vision and business needs
  • Prioritize backlog (ordered list of features)
  • Validates or rejects deliverables at the end of the sprint
  • Interface between business and technology
  • Availability: 20-40% of his dedicated time
Scrum Master (SM)
  • Facilitates rituals and removes obstacles
  • Protects the team from external disturbances
  • Coach the team towards self-organization
  • Guarantor of the Scrum method
  • ⚠️ Attention: This is NOT a project manager!
Dev Team
  • Self-organized (no internal hierarchy)
  • Multidisciplinary (dev, QA, UX if necessary)
  • Ideal size: 5-9 people
  • Collective commitment on the sprint objectives

The 5 Scrum events in detail

1. Sprint Planning (2-4h for a 2-week sprint)
  • Part 1: What will we deliver? (Sprint Goal)
  • Part 2: How are we going to do it? (Technical breakdown)
  • Output: Sprint Backlog (list of sprint tasks)
2. Daily Scrum / Stand-up (15 min max, standing)
  • Same time, same place, every day
  • 3 questions per person:
* What did I do yesterday? * What will I do today? * Do I have blockages?
  • ⚠️ This is NOT a report to the boss, but a team synchronization
3. Sprint Review (1-2h)
  • Feature Demo Completed
  • Feedback from the PO and stakeholders
  • Product Backlog adjustment if necessary
4. Sprint Retrospective (1-2h)
  • Time to think about the process
  • 3 key questions:
* What worked well? * What went wrong? * What improvement action for the next sprint?
  • Format: Start / Stop / Continue
5. Backlog Refinement (1-2h per week)
  • Refining future user stories
  • Estimate (Planning Poker, T-shirt sizing)
  • Clarification of acceptance criteria

Scrum Artifacts

  • Product Backlog: Prioritized list of everything that remains to be done
  • Sprint Backlog: Tasks selected for the current sprint
  • Increment: Functional version of the product at the end of the sprint

Useful metrics

  • Velocity: Number of story points delivered per sprint
  • Burndown Chart: Still to do vs time
  • Cycle Time: Average time to complete a story
✅ Benefits of Scrum
  • Clear and structured framework
  • Full transparency on progress
  • Fast and regular feedback
  • Integrated continuous improvement
❌ Scrum Limitations
  • May seem cumbersome for very small teams
  • Requires commitment from the entire team
  • Risk of "Scrum Theater" without real agility

2️⃣ Kanban: fluidity as a philosophy

Origin and principles

Kanban comes from the Toyota production system (1940s). Applied to dev in 2007 by David Anderson. 4 fundamental principles:
  • Start with your current process
  • Agree to gradually pursue evolutionary change
  • Respect current roles and responsibilities
  • Encourage leadership at all levels

The Kanban board

Typical columns: ``` | Backlog | To do | In analysis | In development | In testing | In review | Done | ``` WIP Limit (Work In Progress)
  • Example: Max 3 dev tasks simultaneously
  • Objective: finish what is started before taking on more
  • Reveals bottlenecks

Kanban Metrics

  • Lead Time: Total time from "Backlog" to "Done"
  • Cycle Time: Time from "In Progress" to "Done"
  • Throughput: Number of tasks completed per week
  • Cumulative Flow Diagram: Visualization of flows

Key practices

1. View workflow
  • Everything must be visible on the board
  • Color code by type (feature, bug, tech debt)
2. Limit WIP
  • Force to finish before starting
  • Reveals crashes
3. Manage flow
  • Measure and optimize cycle time
  • Identify bottlenecks
4. Make rules explicit
  • Definition of Done by column
  • Criteria for moving from one column to another
5. Collaborative improvement
  • Regular retrospectives (even without sprint)
✅ Benefits of Kanban
  • Very flexible, no timeboxing
  • Easy to implement gradually
  • Clear visualization of the work
  • Suitable for support/maintenance teams
❌ Kanban Limits
  • May lack pace without sprints
  • Requires strong discipline
  • Less predictability than with Scrum

3️⃣ XP (Extreme Programming): technical excellence

The 5 XP values

  • Communication: constant dialogue within the team
  • Simplicity: make the simplest thing that works
  • Feedback: quick and frequent feedback
  • Courage: dare to refactor, tell the truth
  • Respect: between team members

The 12 XP practices

Development practices: 1. Test-Driven Development (TDD)
  • Write test before code
  • Red-Green-Refactor Cycle
  • High code coverage
2. Pair Programming
  • 2 devs, 1 keyboard
  • Driver (code) + Navigator (reflects)
  • Regular rotation
  • Instant knowledge sharing
3. Continuous refactoring
  • Improve the code without changing its behavior
  • Keep code clean at all times
  • Minimum technical debt
4. Simple code
  • YAGNI: You Aren't Gonna Need It
  • No over-engineering
5. Collective ownership of code
  • Anyone can edit any part
  • No silos
6. Code Standards
  • Common Conventions
  • Auto Linting
  • Code reviews
Management practices: 7. Continuous integration
  • Merges on hand several times per day
  • Automatic build and testing
8. Frequent deliveries
  • Short releases (1-2 weeks)
  • Quick user feedback
9. Sustainable pace
  • No more than 40 hours/week
  • No regular overtime
10. On-premises client
  • Product Owner available
  • Quick answers to questions
11. Planning Game
  • Estimate in story points
  • Prioritization by customer
12. Metaphor
  • Shared vision of the system
  • Common vocabulary

Complementarity with Scrum

XP focuses on how to develop (technical practices). Scrum focuses on how to organize (management framework). Winning combo: Scrum + XP
  • Scrum for the organizational framework
  • XP for technical excellence
✅ Benefits of XP
  • Exceptional code quality
  • Very few bugs in production
  • United and competent team
  • Almost zero technical debt
❌ XP Limits
  • Demanding and disciplined
  • Resource-intensive pair programming
  • Requires an experienced team
  • Customer must be very available

🔄 Comparison and choice

| Criterion | Scrum | Kanban | XP | |--------|-------|--------|---------| | Structure | Rigid | Flexible | Very rigid | | Timeboxing | Yes (sprints) | No | Yes (iterations) | | Roles | 3 defined roles | No imposed role | Everyone dev | | Changes | End of sprint | Anytime | End of iteration | | Focus | Project management | Continuous flow | Tech excellence | | Learning curve | Average | Easy | Difficult | | Suitable for | Product projects | Support/maintenance | Critical projects |

🎯 How to choose?

Starts with Scrum if:
  • New agility team
  • Need clear framework
  • Produced project with regular releases
Adopts Kanban if:
  • Continuous workflow (support, ops)
  • No fixed release cycles
  • Smooth transition from waterfall
Uses XP if:
  • Critical quality (finance, health, aero)
  • Senior and motivated team
  • Very involved customer
Combine Scrum + XP if:
  • Complex project
  • Need for framework AND technical excellence
  • Mature team

🚀 Where to start?

Week 1: Understand

  • Read the Agile Manifesto
  • Watch videos on Scrum/Kanban
  • Identify your current team's problems

Week 2: Experiment

  • Choose ONE framework (Scrum recommended to start)
  • Train the team (certified Scrum Master if possible)
  • Define roles

Week 3: Launch

  • First 2-week sprint
  • All Scrum rituals
  • Measure velocity

Week 4: Adjust

  • First serious retrospective
  • Identify 1-2 improvements
  • Iterate

📚 Resources to go further

Essential books:
  • "Scrum: The Art of Doing Twice the Work in Half the Time" - Jeff Sutherland
  • "Kanban: Successful Evolutionary Change" - David Anderson
  • "Extreme Programming Explained" - Kent Beck
Useful certifications:
  • PSM I (Professional Scrum Master) - Scrum.org
  • PSPO I (Professional Scrum Product Owner)
  • KMP (Kanban Management Professional)
Recommended tools:
  • Jira, Linear, Azure DevOps (Scrum)
  • Trello, Notion, Monday (Kanban)
  • GitHub Projects (simple and free)

⚠️ Pitfalls to avoid

❌ Scrum Zombie: doing the rituals without the agile mind ❌ Anarchic Kanban: no WIP limit = chaos ❌ XP without tests: pair programming alone is not enough ❌ Theoretical agility: talking agile without delivering regularly ❌ Micro-management: agility is not control in disguise

🧩 Conclusion

> Scrum structures your organization. > Kanban streamlines your workflow. > XP solidifies your technical base. Agility is not a magic recipe, but a working philosophy. Start small, experiment, measure, adjust. Success is not in the chosen framework, but in the continuous improvement mindset of your team. Next step: Choose a framework, form your team, launch a first sprint/cycle, and learn from your mistakes. Agility is experienced, not read! 🚀

title: How to write good User Stories
content:
Introduction

User Stories are the basis of communication between business and technology. They replace rigid specifications with simple, user-centered language.

Structure of a User Story

> As [user role], I want [objective] in order to [benefit / added value]. Examples:
  • As a user, I want to be able to reset my password in order to regain access to my account.
  • As an administrator, I want to filter users by status in order to manage active accounts more quickly.

Acceptance Criteria (Definition of Done)

These are the conditions that define when the story is “finished”. Example for password reset:
  • The user receives an email containing a unique link.
  • The link expires after 24 hours.
  • The password must contain at least 8 characters.
👉 These criteria serve as a basis for testing and ensure shared understanding.

INVEST rule

A good story should be:
  • Independent
  • Nnegotiable
  • Valorizing
  • Estimable
  • Simple
  • Tstable

Common errors

❌ Too many technical details. ❌ Story too big (“Epic”) uncut. ❌ Lack of testing criteria.

Conclusion

A well-written user story is clear communication and shared product vision.

title: The 5 pillars of TDD (Test Driven Development)
content:
Introduction

TDD, or test-driven development, is a method that reverses the usual logic: > We write the tests before the code.

The “Red – Green – Refactor” cycle

  • Red → Write a test which fails (expected behavior).
  • Green → Write the minimal code to pass the test.
  • Refactor → Cleans up the code without breaking the tests.

The 5 pillars of TDD

  • Short cycles: Write a test every 2–5 minutes.
  • Isolated unit tests: no external dependencies.
  • Frequent refactoring: keeps the code simple.
  • Confidence in code: you edit without fear.
  • Immediate feedback: instantly visible errors.

Simple example

```python def add(a, b): return a + b def test_add(): assert add(2, 3) == 5 ``` You first create `test_add()` before even writing `add()`.

Benefits

✅ Drastically reduced bugs. ✅ Solid foundation for refactoring. ✅ Living documentation.

Conclusion

TDD is a developer safety net: it forces you to think before you act.

title: How to organize a sprint effectively
content:
Introduction

A well-managed sprint = a project that is moving forward. The goal: deliver a concrete increment at each iteration.

Steps of a successful sprint

1. Sprint Planning

  • Define a clear objective (e.g.: "deliver the user profile page").
  • Estimate the stories together (Planning Poker).

2. Daily Stand-up

  • 3 simple questions: What did I do? What am I going to do? Am I stuck?

3. Sprint Review

  • Shows completed features.
  • Collects customer feedback.

4. Sprint Retrospective

  • Analyzes what worked and what didn't.
  • Choose 1 area of improvement for the next sprint.

Common errors

❌ Too many undelivered stories. ❌ Blurry sprint goal. ❌ No improvement between sprints.

Recommended tools

  • Jira, Trello, Linear, Notion
  • GitHub Projects for small projects
  • Burndown chart to view progress

Conclusion

A sprint is a continuous learning framework: the team grows as much as the product.

title: Code Review: best practices for giving (and receiving) feedback
content:
Introduction

The Code Review is not just a quality check: it is a collective learning opportunity.

Objectives

  • Improve code quality.
  • Share knowledge.
  • Prevent bugs and technical debt.

Reviewer best practices

✅ Be constructive: criticize the code, not the person. ✅ Comments in a precise and justified manner. ✅ Prioritizes critical points: security, readability, performance. ✅ Encourages good practices (“great idea here 👍”).

Best practices from the author

✅ Prepare a clear pull request: small scope, good description. ✅ Provide context ("This change fixes bug #42"). ✅ Respond with respect and openness.

Useful tools

  • GitHub / GitLab PRs
  • ReviewPad / CodeScene
  • ESLint + Prettier for auto attendants

Conclusion

A good review is a discussion between peers, not a judgment. It is the basis of a team that progresses together.

title: Why documenting your code is a superpower
content:
Introduction

Documentation is often seen as a chore... until the day you take over a six-month-old project and bless the person who took the time to write two lines. Documenting your code means thinking about your "future self" and your team.

Why document?

  • Save time in the long run - A good doc saves hours of code reading.
  • Improve transmission - You facilitate the onboarding of new members.
  • Clarify your own choices - Explaining your code already means analyzing it.
  • Serve the customer - What you deliver must be able to be understood without your intervention.

Types of documentation

  • README.md: project overview (installation, execution, contribution).
  • Comments in code: the *why*, not the *how*.
  • Technical Wiki: decisions, architecture diagrams, APIs.
  • Changelog: follow developments and releases.
  • Self-generated Doc: JSDoc, Doxygen, Sphinx.

Best practices

✅ Write the doc during development, not after the fact. ✅ Use a clear, concise, professional tone. ✅ Update the doc with each code change. ✅ Documents *processes*, not just code.

Useful tools

  • Markdown (simple and universal)
  • GitHub Pages to host your doc
  • Notion or Obsidian
  • Swagger / Postman for APIs

Conclusion

> "Good code is readable. Excellent code is understood thanks to its documentation."

title: How to refactor without breaking everything
content:
Introduction

Refactoring is improving the structure of the code without changing its behavior. This is essential for the health of the project, but dangerous if done poorly.

Why refactor?

  • To simplify code that has become complex.
  • To improve performance.
  • To make the code more readable and maintainable.
  • To prepare a new feature properly.

Methodology

  • Secure with testing: Good refactoring relies on a solid testing foundation.
  • Changes in small steps: Never refactor everything at once.
  • Uses atomic commits: one change = one intention.
  • Measurement before/after: complexity, performance, readability.

Common refactoring types

  • Extract a function: split long blocks into clear subfunctions.
  • Rename variables or classes to make more sense.
  • Remove dead or duplicate code.
  • Isolate dependencies (injection, adapter pattern).

Errors to avoid

❌ Refactor without testing. ❌ Change functional behavior by mistake. ❌ Strive for “perfection” instead of clarity.

Useful tools

  • IDE: IntelliJ, VS Code, PyCharm
  • Analysers: SonarQube, ESLint, Flake8
  • Automated unit tests

Conclusion

Refactoring means doing preventative maintenance. Code that is refactored regularly ages better and costs less in the long run.

title: The 10 commandments of clean code
content:
Introduction

*Clean Code*, popularized by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"), is a philosophy: writing code that is simple, readable and scalable.

The 10 commandments

  • Your code will be readable before being optimized.
  • You will clearly name your variables and functions.
  • You will avoid code duplication.
  • You will test what you write.
  • You will not add anything unnecessary.
  • You will refactor regularly.
  • You will respect the coherence of your project.
  • You will only comment when necessary.
  • You will trust your linter.
  • You will seek simplicity, not perfection.

Concrete example

❌ Bad: ```js function p(u, v) { return u + v; } ``` ✅ Clean: ```js function addUserScore(baseScore, bonus) { return baseScore + bonus; } ```

Why it matters

  • Readability = fewer bugs.
  • Maintainability = time savings in the long term.
  • Consistency = less friction as a team.

Tools that help

  • ESLint / Prettier (JS)
  • Pylint / Black (Python)
  • SonarQube / Code Climate

Conclusion

> "Clean Code is not written by following rules. It's written by following care."

title: How to properly name your variables and functions
content:
Introduction

A good name is self-explanatory. This is often what differentiates an amateur code from a professional code.

Golden rules

  • Clarity before conciseness: `isAuthenticatedUser` > `usrAuth`.
  • Verbs for functions, names for variables.
  • Constance in the conventions: `camelCase` or `snake_case`, but not both.
  • No obscure abbreviations: `nbUsrActv` is unreadable.
  • No redundant context: `user.userName` → `user.name`.

Examples

❌ `d = Date.now()` → we don't know what it is. ✅ `createdAt = Date.now()` → instantly understandable. ❌ `processData(data)` ✅ `normalizeUserInput(userFormData)`

Little tips

  • Named according to the "what" and "why", not the "how".
  • Imagine someone reads your code without context.
  • Names must last longer than the dev's memory.

Conventions by language

  • JavaScript / Java / C# → camelCase for variables, PascalCase for classes.
  • Python / Ruby → snake_case.
  • CSS → kebab-case.

Conclusion

Naming is thinking business logic. A good name tells a story: it makes your code self-documenting.

title: Automate your repetitive tasks: introduction to the DevOps mindset
content:
Introduction

The DevOps reflex is: > “If you do the same thing three times, automate it.” Automating means increasing productivity and reducing human errors.

Why automate?

  • Fewer omissions and manual errors.
  • Save time on tasks without added value.
  • Create a reliable build, test and deployment pipeline.

Concrete examples

  • Automate tests before each commit → via Git hooks or GitHub Actions.
  • Continuous deployment → CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI).
  • Automatic cleanup → script to remove merged branches.
  • Automatic documentation generation → Swagger, Typedoc, Doxygen.
  • Backup and automatic monitoring → Cron jobs, alerting, monitoring.

Essential tools

  • Makefile / Taskfile → for recurring orders.
  • Bash / PowerShell scripts → to automate locally.
  • Docker + Compose → to standardize environments.
  • CI/CD (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) → to orchestrate it all.

Simple example (Makefile)

```makefile test: pytest tests/ deploy: git push origin main gh workflow run deploy.yml ``` A command `make deploy` and your code goes into production 🚀

Conclusion

Automation is the key to technical peace of mind. This is the essence of DevOps: reliability, efficiency and confidence in your pipeline.

title: Pair Programming & Mob Programming: coding with others
content:
Introduction: Collaborative programming

Solo development is good, but coding with others is better! Proven benefits:
  • -60% bugs in production
  • Real-time review code
  • Immediate knowledge transfer
  • Onboarding 3x faster

🤝 Pair Programming

The Driver/Navigator model

Driver (the one who types):
  • Writes code
  • Think about tactical implementation
  • Explains what it does
Navigator (the one who observes):
  • Think about the overall strategy
  • Anticipate problems
  • Search documentation
  • Ask questions

Pairing techniques

1. Ping Pong Pairing (with TDD)
  • Dev A: Writes a test that fails
  • Dev B: Takes the test
  • Dev B: Write the next test
  • Dev A: Takes the test
  • Continuous rotation!
2. Strong-Style Pairing “For an idea to get from your head to the keyboard, it has to pass through someone else’s hands.”
  • The Navigator dictates
  • The Driver executes
  • Rotation every 5-10 min

👥 Mob Programming

The principle

The whole team on the same problem at the same time
  • 1 Driver (which codes)
  • 3-6 Navigators (which guide)
  • 1 split screen (wide screen or screen split)
  • Rotation every 10-15 min

When to use Mob Programming?

Use case:
  • Complex architecture to decide
  • Urgent critical bug
  • Onboarding of a new dev
  • Technical Spike (Exploration)
  • Legacy code difficult to understand

⚙️ Technical setup

Local pairing

Option 1: Live Share (VS Code)
  • Free extension
  • Terminal sharing included
  • Integrated Audio/Video
  • Multi-color cursors
Option 2: tmux (terminal) Shared SSH session for purists!

Pairing remote

Recommended tools:
  • Tuple: Excellent for remote pairing
  • Pop: Optimized Screensharing dev
  • VS Code Live Share: Free and simple

✅ Best practices

For the Driver

  • Think out loud
  • Don't hesitate to ask for advice
  • Take regular breaks
  • Accept suggestions

For the Navigator

  • Be patient, let the Driver type
  • Ask questions instead of imposing
  • Search for doc while Driver codes
  • Take notes of ideas to explore

🚀 Putting it into practice

Start with short sessions of 1-2 hours, then gradually increase. Pair programming is not for all day every day! Schedule type:
  • Morning: Pairing on complex features (2h)
  • Afternoon: Solo work (code reviews, docs)
  • Friday: Mob programming on architecture (1h)
Collaboration makes the code better and the team stronger! 🤝

title: Continuous learning: staying up to date in tech
content:
Introduction: Tech never stops

New framework every month, new best practices, new languages... How to stay up to date without spending 10 hours a day?

📚 The 5 pillars of lifelong learning

1. Learn by doing (80% of the time)

Side projects
  • 1 new project every 2-3 months
  • Use a technology you don't know
  • Published on GitHub
Coding challenges
  • LeetCode / HackerRank (algo)
  • Advent of Code (fun and challenging)
  • CodeWars (daily katas)

2. Read and watch (15% of the time)

Essential newsletters
  • TLDR: Daily tech news
  • JavaScript Weekly: Front-end
  • Bytes.dev: React/JS fun
  • Pointer: Engineering best practices
Blogs to follow
  • Kent C. Dodds (React, Testing)
  • Martin Fowler (Architecture)
  • CSS Tricks (Front-end)
  • Dev.to (community)

3. Contribute open-source (3% of the time)

How to get started:
  • Fix the documentation of a project you are using
  • Looks for "good first issue"
  • Reports bugs with clear reproduction

4. Teach and share (2% of the time)

The best way to learn = teach
  • Write articles (dev.to, Medium)
  • Do internal talks
  • Answers on Stack Overflow
  • Creates YouTube tutorials

⏰ Realistic sleep schedule

Daily (15-30 min)

  • Reading newsletter during coffee ☕
  • 1 technical article
  • Quick scroll Twitter/Reddit tech

Weekly (2-3h)

  • 1 video tutorial (YouTube, Egghead.io)
  • Working on side project
  • Read 1 chapter of a technical book

Monthly (1 day)

  • Participate in a meetup/conference
  • Refactor an old side project
  • Explore new technology in depth

🎯 Choose what to learn

The learning matrix

Priority 1: Useful AND interesting
  • Technology used in your current job
  • Skill that can open doors for you
Priority 2: Useful but not interesting
  • Learn the minimum necessary
  • Delegate if possible
Priority 3: Interesting but not useful
  • For fun, as a side project
  • No pressure

📖 Learning Resources

Fundamental Technical Books

  • Clean Code - Robert Martin
  • The Pragmatic Programmer - Hunt & Thomas
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Kleppmann
  • You Don't Know JS - Kyle Simpson

Learning platforms

  • Frontend Masters: Advanced front-end courses
  • Egghead.io: Short and dense videos
  • Pluralsight: Huge catalog
  • Exercism: Learn by coding

💡 Pro Tips

Learning in public

Document what you learn on Twitter, blog, GitHub. Benefits:
  • You remember better
  • You help other people
  • You create a portfolio
  • You attract opportunities

The 8 p.m. rule

20 hours of deliberate practice is enough to go from beginner to proficient at a topic.
  • Week 1-2: Basic Tutorials
  • Week 3-4: Build something concrete
  • After: You are operational!

🚫 Pitfalls to avoid

Tutorial Hell

Make endless tutorials without ever building real projects. Solution: 1 tutorial = 1 personal project applied

Imposter Syndrome

"I don't know enough..." Reality: Nobody knows everything. Even seniors learn every day.

Shiny Object Syndrome

Running after every new trendy technology. Solution: Master the fundamentals before changing.

🎓 Action Plan

  • Choose 1 skill to develop this month
  • Block 30 minutes a day in your calendar
  • Build 1 mini-project in 2 weeks
  • Share your learning (Twitter, blog)
  • Repeat next month with a new skill
Continuous learning is not a sprint, it's a marathon. Stay curious, stay humble, and code! 🚀
